uses: Chest pain and pulmonary edema in acute MI
quickTip: Hold and notify the provider if respirations are under 12/min or the patient is hard to arouse. Naloxone stays at the bedside.
administration: IV push slowly over 4-5 minutes; extended-release tablets are swallowed whole, never crushed, chewed, or split.
mechanism: Binds mu-opioid receptors in the spinal cord and brain, blocking pain signals from being passed along and changing how the brain experiences them.
simplified: Turns the pain signal's volume down before the brain hears it.
nursing: Assess pain, respiratory rate, and sedation level before every dose; sedation shows up before respiratory depression.
Start a bowel regimen (stool softener plus stimulant) from day one - tolerance to constipation never develops.
Check BP and use fall precautions; orthostatic drops are common early on.
No alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants.
Expect tolerance and physical dependence with long-term use; taper rather than stop abruptly.

quickTip: Naloxone wears off in 30-90 minutes, sooner than most opioids, so the patient can re-sedate. Plan on repeat doses and continued monitoring.
administration: IV push, IM, subcutaneous, or intranasal spray; repeat every 2-3 minutes until respirations improve.
mechanism: Competes for the same mu receptors as opioids and displaces them, reversing sedation and respiratory depression within 1-2 minutes IV.
simplified: The bouncer that throws opioids off their receptors.
nursing: Support ventilation first; naloxone is added to airway management, not a substitute for it.
Monitor RR, SpO2, and LOC every 15 minutes for at least 2 hours after the last dose.
Expect sudden pain and acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients; titrate to breathing, not full alertness.
Teach families of at-risk patients to use the nasal spray, place the person on their side, and call 911.

quickTip: Maximum 4 g/day, or 3 g/day in older adults and liver disease. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for overdose.
administration: PO, rectal, or IV over 15 minutes; count the acetaminophen hidden in combination cold and opioid products toward the daily limit.
mechanism: Blocks prostaglandin production mainly inside the central nervous system, lowering pain and fever with almost no anti-inflammatory effect in the body.
simplified: Pain and fever relief without the stomach or bleeding problems of NSAIDs.
nursing: Add up every source of acetaminophen the patient takes before giving a dose.
Ask about alcohol use; 3 or more drinks a day sharply raises liver risk.
Overdose symptoms are delayed: RUQ pain, jaundice, dark urine, and nausea appear 24-72 hours later.
Does not reduce inflammation or affect platelets, so it is the safer choice with anticoagulants - but regular high doses can raise INR on warfarin.

quickTip: Take with food and avoid in kidney disease, GI bleeding history, heart failure, and after 20 weeks of pregnancy.
administration: PO with food, milk, or a full glass of water; IV form infuses over 30 minutes.
mechanism: Blocks COX-1 and COX-2, cutting prostaglandin production that drives pain, fever, and inflammation - and also the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and kidney.
simplified: Less prostaglandin means less pain and swelling, but also less stomach lining protection.
nursing: Report black tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis, or unusual bruising.
Check BUN, creatinine, and BP with regular use; NSAIDs shrink kidney blood flow.
Avoid combining with warfarin, other NSAIDs, or corticosteroids; can blunt low-dose aspirin's heart protection.
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time; OTC use should not exceed 10 days without checking in.

uses: Short-term moderate to severe acute pain
quickTip: Maximum 5 days total across all routes - the GI bleed and kidney injury risk climbs steeply after that.
administration: IM, IV over at least 15 seconds, PO, or nasal spray; PO is only for continuing a course started IV/IM. Never beyond day 5.
mechanism: A strong COX inhibitor that shuts down prostaglandin production, delivering opioid-level pain relief without sedation or respiratory depression.
simplified: Opioid-strength relief from an NSAID, rationed to 5 days.
nursing: Contraindicated with active GI bleeding, kidney impairment, before major surgery, in labor and delivery, and with other NSAIDs or aspirin.
Check creatinine and make sure the patient is hydrated before dosing.
Older adults and patients under 50 kg get the reduced 15 mg dose.
Do not give with anticoagulants; watch for bleeding at surgical sites.

quickTip: Ask about penicillin allergy before the first dose and teach patients to finish the entire course even once they feel better.
administration: PO with or without food; shake the suspension well, refrigerate it, and discard after 14 days.
mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins and blocks the cross-linking of the bacterial cell wall, so the wall weakens and the cell bursts.
simplified: Pokes holes in the bacterial wall so it can't hold itself together.
nursing: Hives, wheezing, or facial swelling means stop the drug and treat for anaphylaxis; a flat non-itchy rash in a patient with mono is common and not a true allergy.
About 1-2% cross-reactivity with cephalosporins; check the allergy history carefully.
Report watery or bloody diarrhea - possible C. diff; do not self-treat with antidiarrheals.
Space doses evenly around the clock and complete the full course to prevent resistance.

quickTip: Draw the trough right before the 4th dose (goal 10-20 mcg/mL) and infuse over at least 60 minutes to prevent red man syndrome.
administration: IV over 60 minutes or longer for bigger doses; oral capsules are only for C. diff because the drug is not absorbed from the gut.
mechanism: Binds the building blocks of the gram-positive cell wall so they can't be assembled, and the bacterium dies.
simplified: Grabs the bricks so the bacterial wall never gets built.
nursing: Monitor BUN, creatinine, and urine output; avoid pairing with aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, loop diuretics, or contrast.
Ask about tinnitus or hearing loss at each shift; ototoxicity can be permanent.
Flushing and itching of the face, neck, and chest during infusion: slow or pause the drip, give diphenhydramine, then restart slower.
Assess the IV site - vancomycin is irritating and causes phlebitis.
IV vancomycin does not treat C. diff; the oral form does.

uses: Serious gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas, E. coli, Klebsiella)
quickTip: Peaks and troughs are required: trough right before the dose, peak 30 minutes after the infusion ends. A rising trough means kidney and ear damage is coming.
administration: IV over 30-60 minutes or IM; trough goal under 2 mcg/mL with conventional dosing, or once-daily extended-interval dosing.
mechanism: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit so bacteria build faulty proteins; needs oxygen to enter the cell, so it does nothing against anaerobes.
nursing: Check creatinine, BUN, and urine output daily and keep the patient well hydrated.
Ask about tinnitus, hearing changes, or dizziness every shift; damage to the 8th cranial nerve is often irreversible.
Avoid other nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs: vancomycin, loop diuretics, NSAIDs, cisplatin.
Enhances neuromuscular blockers; use with caution in myasthenia gravis.
Baseline audiogram for courses longer than a week.

uses: Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever
quickTip: Causes photosensitivity, binds to dairy, antacids, and iron, and is avoided in pregnancy and children under 8 because it stains teeth and slows bone growth.
administration: PO with a full glass of water, staying upright for 30 minutes to prevent esophageal burns; separate from calcium, iron, magnesium, and antacids by 2 hours.
mechanism: Binds the 30S ribosome to stop bacterial protein production; it is bacteriostatic, so the immune system finishes the job.
simplified: Pauses the bacterial protein line so the body's defenses can catch up.
nursing: Sunscreen, hats, and long sleeves; sunburn can happen within minutes of exposure.
Taking it with food is acceptable if it upsets the stomach - just not with dairy.
Never take expired tetracyclines; breakdown products damage the kidney.
Report severe diarrhea, vaginal itching, or white patches in the mouth.
Confirm the patient is not pregnant or breastfeeding before starting.

quickTip: Stop the drug and report tendon pain or swelling at once - Achilles rupture risk is highest in older adults and anyone on corticosteroids. Also prolongs the QT interval.
administration: PO or IV over 60 minutes; take 2 hours before or 6 hours after antacids, calcium, iron, zinc, or dairy, and drink plenty of fluids.
mechanism: Blocks DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV so bacteria can't unwind and copy their DNA - bactericidal.
simplified: Locks the bacterial DNA so it can't be copied.
nursing: Avoid in myasthenia gravis, with other QT-prolonging drugs, and in patients at risk for aortic aneurysm.
Monitor blood glucose closely in diabetics; both hypo- and hyperglycemia occur.
Encourage 2-3 L of fluid a day to prevent crystals in the urine.
Report numbness, tingling, mood changes, or tendon pain - these can be lasting.
Raises theophylline and warfarin levels; not a first choice in children or pregnancy.

quickTip: No alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after - a disulfiram-like reaction causes flushing, vomiting, and pounding headache. A metallic taste is expected and harmless.
administration: PO with food to limit GI upset; IV over 30-60 minutes; extended-release tablets on an empty stomach.
mechanism: Enters anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, where their low-oxygen chemistry activates it into a form that breaks DNA strands.
simplified: Only anaerobes can switch it on, and then it shreds their DNA.
nursing: Screen for alcohol in mouthwash, cough syrups, and tinctures - not just drinks.
Warn that dark or reddish-brown urine is harmless.
Sexual partners need treatment too for trichomoniasis; avoid intercourse until both finish.
Report numbness or tingling in the hands and feet; stop the drug if it appears.
Boosts warfarin's effect - monitor INR.

quickTip: Red-orange urine, sweat, tears, and saliva are harmless but stain soft contact lenses. Hormonal contraceptives fail - use a backup method.
administration: PO on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, with a full glass of water; IV over 30 minutes to 3 hours.
mechanism: Blocks bacterial RNA polymerase so the mycobacterium can't transcribe its genes into RNA.
simplified: Breaks the copy machine that turns bacterial DNA into RNA.
nursing: Baseline and monthly liver tests; report jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain, or loss of appetite.
Powerful CYP450 inducer - lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, HIV drugs, and many others; review every medication.
Never used alone for active TB; resistance develops fast. Teach adherence for the full 6-9 months.
No alcohol; it compounds the liver risk of the other TB drugs.
Remove soft contact lenses for the duration of therapy.

quickTip: Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to prevent peripheral neuropathy, watch the liver, and no alcohol.
administration: PO on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals; separate from aluminum antacids by at least 1 hour. IM is available.
mechanism: Blocks production of mycolic acid, the waxy material the mycobacterial cell wall is built from, killing actively dividing TB bacteria.
simplified: Stops TB from making the wax its wall is made of.
nursing: Baseline and periodic LFTs; hold and report jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, or loss of appetite - hepatitis risk rises with age and alcohol use.
Pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily prevents numbness and tingling in the hands and feet.
Slow acetylators build higher levels and more toxicity; ask about unusual drowsiness or neuropathy.
Avoid tyramine- and histamine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, tuna) - flushing, headache, and palpitations can result.
Raises phenytoin and carbamazepine levels; adherence for 6-9 months, often by directly observed therapy.

uses: Adjunct to shift potassium into cells in hyperkalemia
quickTip: This is the rescue inhaler and it goes first, before any inhaled steroid. Needing it more than twice a week means the asthma is not controlled.
administration: MDI: shake, exhale fully, inhale slowly while pressing, hold breath 10 seconds, wait 1 minute between puffs; use a spacer. Nebulizer over 5-15 minutes.
mechanism: Stimulates beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, relaxing the airways within minutes.
simplified: Flips the beta-2 switch that opens the airways fast.
nursing: Give albuterol first, wait about 5 minutes, then the inhaled corticosteroid so it reaches opened airways.
Check heart rate before and after; report chest pain, a rate over 120, or symptoms that don't ease - paradoxical bronchospasm is possible.
Caution with heart disease, hyperthyroidism, and diabetes; limit caffeine.
Nonselective beta-blockers (propranolol) cancel its effect.
Teach dose counting so the canister isn't empty during an attack.

uses: Add-on to albuterol in severe asthma attacks
quickTip: Onset is about 15 minutes, so it is not a stand-alone rescue inhaler. Expect dry mouth and keep the mist out of the eyes - blurred vision and glaucoma risk.
administration: MDI or nebulizer, often mixed with albuterol; use a mouthpiece rather than a face mask when possible and rinse the mouth afterward.
mechanism: Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airways so acetylcholine can't tighten bronchial muscle or drive mucus production.
simplified: Blocks the squeeze signal so the airways stay open.
nursing: Use with caution in narrow-angle glaucoma, BPH, or urinary retention; report eye pain or trouble urinating.
Sips of water or sugarless gum for dry mouth; rinse after each use.
Not for acute rescue on its own - pair with albuterol for fast relief.
Little systemic absorption, so it is well tolerated even with heart disease.

uses: Reducing exacerbations and rescue inhaler use
quickTip: Not a rescue inhaler - full effect takes 1-2 weeks. Rinse the mouth and spit after every use to prevent thrush.
administration: Inhaled on a fixed schedule even when symptom-free; if albuterol is also due, give albuterol first, then use a spacer for the steroid, then rinse and spit.
mechanism: Acts inside airway cells to switch off inflammatory gene activity, shrinking swelling, mucus, and airway twitchiness over days.
simplified: Calms the airway inflammation so attacks happen less often.
nursing: Inspect the mouth for white patches; a spacer plus rinse-and-spit cuts thrush and hoarseness.
Never stop abruptly when switching from oral steroids - adrenal insufficiency can follow.
Track growth in children on long-term therapy.
Report if the rescue inhaler is needed more often - the controller dose may need adjusting.

quickTip: Take 30-60 minutes before breakfast and swallow capsules whole. Long-term use raises the risk of C. diff, fractures, low magnesium, and B12 deficiency.
administration: PO before the first meal of the day; delayed-release capsules can be opened and the pellets sprinkled on applesauce, but never chewed or crushed.
mechanism: Permanently shuts down the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump in stomach parietal cells - the final step in acid production - until new pumps are made.
simplified: Unplugs the acid pump itself, so almost no acid gets made.
nursing: Give before meals because the pump has to be active for the drug to bind it.
Reassess the need after 8 weeks and use the lowest effective dose.
Check magnesium and B12 with use beyond a year.
Blunts clopidogrel activation; pantoprazole is preferred in that combination.
Taper rather than stop cold - rebound acid is common.

uses: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critical care
quickTip: Faster but weaker than a PPI. Reduce the dose in kidney disease, where it can cause confusion - especially in older adults.
administration: PO with or without food, often at bedtime; IV push over at least 2 minutes or infusion over 15-30 minutes.
mechanism: Blocks H2 receptors on parietal cells so histamine can't tell them to make acid, cutting output by about 70%, mostly at night.
simplified: Blocks histamine's make-acid message to the stomach.
nursing: Bedtime dosing best controls nighttime acid.
Dose adjustment when CrCl is under 50 mL/min; monitor mental status in older adults.
Tolerance builds with daily use, so PPIs are preferred for erosive disease.
Far fewer drug interactions than cimetidine.
OTC use beyond 2 weeks or trouble swallowing means see a provider.

quickTip: Always a secondary line on an infusion pump, never the primary. For tachysystole (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes) or late decelerations: stop the drip, turn mom to her side, give oxygen and a fluid bolus, notify the provider.
administration: Dilute in isotonic fluid (e.g. 30 units in 500 mL LR) and titrate in milliunits per minute by pump; after delivery it runs faster, or 10 units IM.
mechanism: Binds oxytocin receptors on uterine muscle, raising calcium inside the cells so contractions come stronger and more often; also triggers milk let-down.
simplified: Tells the uterus to squeeze - and keeps saying it as long as the pump runs.
nursing: Continuous fetal heart rate and contraction monitoring; reassess before every rate increase, usually every 30-60 minutes.
Stop for tachysystole, contractions longer than 90 seconds, resting tone above 20 mmHg, or a non-reassuring FHR.
Strict I&O; watch for headache, confusion, falling urine output, and seizures from water intoxication with prolonged high-dose infusions.
Contraindicated with placenta previa, cephalopelvic disproportion, prior classical uterine incision, or active genital herpes.
Postpartum: check fundal tone and lochia; oxytocin is given after the placenta delivers, not before.
